title: Introducing Alternate Futures: The Decentralized Cloud for AI Agents
excerpt: We built Alternate Futures because the cloud should not have a single point of failure. Here is the platform we are building for AI agents, full-stack apps, and static sites on decentralized infrastructure.
content: The centralized cloud has served us well, but it comes with trade-offs: vendor lock-in, single regions of failure, and costs that can scale faster than revenue.

Traditional cloud providers concentrate infrastructure in a small number of data centers and regions. A regional outage can affect thousands of products at once. Decentralized infrastructure distributes workloads across independent providers in different locations.
The goal is practical resilience without forcing teams to become infrastructure specialists:
- **Fewer single points of failure** -- workloads can move when individual providers go offline
- **More cost options** -- providers compete for workloads in an open marketplace
- **Infrastructure choice** -- teams can choose where and how their applications run
- **Data sovereignty** -- deployments can be designed around geographic and jurisdictional needs
Alternate Futures is designed to support the range of workloads modern teams need:
| Static sites | Content-addressed storage with global delivery |
| Full-stack apps | Container-based deployment on distributed compute |
| AI agents | Long-running services with persistent state and tool access |
| Background jobs | Scheduled and event-driven workloads |

The product experience should feel familiar: connect a project, choose resources, and deploy. Underneath that workflow, Alternate Futures coordinates providers, certificates, routing, health checks, and billing.
Our direction is a small command-line surface for the common path:

The command-line interface is intended to package the application, select an appropriate provider, configure routing, and return a live deployment URL. Advanced controls remain available when a team needs them, but they should not be required for a first deployment.

AI agents make infrastructure reliability more important, not less. Agents may run continuously, retain state, call external tools, and act on behalf of people. They need an infrastructure layer that is observable, portable, and resistant to a single provider failure.
We are building Alternate Futures around that need while keeping the platform useful for the applications and sites that surround an agent.
Alternate Futures is in active development. [Request early access](https://www.alternatefutures.ai) to follow the work and help shape the platform.
The decentralized cloud will not arrive as a slogan. It will arrive when deploying to it feels ordinary.

title: The Web3 Hosting Vacuum: Why Decentralized Cloud Matters More Than Ever
excerpt: As infrastructure companies shift toward AI compute, Web3 teams still need a simple, reliable path to decentralized hosting.
content: The infrastructure market is moving quickly toward AI compute. That shift is understandable: demand for GPUs is intense, and the economics are attractive. But it leaves an important question for Web3 builders: who is making decentralized application hosting easier?
## The gap is practical, not theoretical
Teams that want to reduce their dependence on a single cloud provider still face a difficult set of choices:
- **Centralized application platforms** are easy to use but keep deployment, billing, and availability inside one vendor
- **Self-managed IPFS** gives teams control but introduces pinning, replication, gateways, and observability work
- **Raw compute marketplaces** provide capacity but ask application teams to assemble the deployment experience themselves
The missing layer is a product that makes distributed infrastructure feel as direct as connecting a repository and pressing deploy.

GPU infrastructure for model training and inference commands premium pricing. Companies that began with decentralized hosting or general-purpose compute have strong incentives to focus on AI workloads.

That does not make web hosting unimportant. Hosting is the foundation underneath decentralized applications, communities, governance tools, and protocols. If publishing and operating those products remains difficult, the ecosystem inherits the same centralization pressure it set out to avoid.
> The decentralized web needs an application layer that is as usable as the centralized alternatives.
Alternate Futures is exploring a unified deployment path for several needs that are currently fragmented across providers.
- Framework-aware builds for common web stacks
- Health checks, logs, and predictable rollbacks
- Persistent state that is not tied to one compute provider
- Secret management and controlled tool access
- One project model across local development and deployment
- A command-line workflow that can also run in CI
- Provider choice without rewriting the application
- An escape hatch for teams that need direct infrastructure control

Decentralization is not a feature badge. It is a set of trade-offs that should be visible to the team operating a product: where the workload runs, who can interrupt it, how data moves, what recovery looks like, and what each provider costs.
A useful platform should expose those choices without making every developer become an infrastructure operator.
The renewed focus on AI infrastructure creates room for a company that cares about the application layer: not only selling compute, but helping teams ship durable software across it.
That is the opportunity Alternate Futures is pursuing. We want decentralized hosting to become a normal engineering choice, supported by good tools and honest operational boundaries.
[Request early access](https://www.alternatefutures.ai) and tell us what you need from a decentralized deployment platform.
